title: Euro Tote Bags Wholesale: Paper GSM, Handle Load & Gusset Sizing
seoTitle: Euro Tote Bags Wholesale: GSM, Handles & Sizing | MTT
summary: Specify custom Euro tote bags for wholesale: choose 210–300 gsm paper stock, 450 gsm bottom boards, knotted cord or ribbon handles, and box-matched gussets.
intro: For wholesale Euro tote bags, match paper weight and handle anchorage to the filled box weight rather than picking the thickest board by default. Most fragrance, skincare, and apparel totes perform reliably on 210–250 gsm C1S art paper with matte lamination, a 450 gsm turnover top and bottom card, and 15–20 mm gusset clearance around the inner rigid box. Always load-test knotted cotton or grosgrain handles with filled product samples before mass production.
faq: What paper GSM is best for wholesale Euro tote bags?

210–250 gsm C1S art paper with matte or soft-touch lamination covers most cosmetics, fragrance, and boutique apparel bags. Move to 270–300 gsm only for oversized bags carrying heavy glass sets or multiple rigid boxes, and pair it with a 450 gsm bottom insert.
How much clearance should I add to a Euro tote gusset for a rigid gift box?
Add 15–20 mm to both the box width and depth for the bag's internal width and side gusset, and at least 35–45 mm above the box top so the handle knots clear the lid without bowing the bag mouth.

sections: Match paper weight and lamination to crease cracking

Euro totes fold sharply along four vertical gussets and a flat-folded bottom. Uncoated or heavily ink-covered 300 gsm boards crack easily along those score lines unless the grain runs vertically and the sheet receives a protective matte or soft-touch film lamination. For dark flood-coated designs—black, navy, or deep burgundy—230–250 gsm C1S art paper with matte BOPP lamination resists fold cracking far better than heavier uncoated card.

If your brand requires an uncoated tactile paper, test the exact dyed stock on a creasing rule during sampling. Pair the bag spec with our custom Euro tote luxury paper bag concept when planning a matching retail set.
Reinforce the turnover top and bottom card

A Euro tote fails at the handle holes or the bottom seam before the side panels tear. Standard construction folds the top edge inward by 35–45 mm over a 450 gsm greyboard or white card reinforcement strip, then punches 5–6 mm eyelets or raw holes for knotted cords. At the base, a separate 450 gsm bottom card distributes point loads from heavy glass bottles so the glued bottom gusset does not sag.
Choose handle attachment for filled weight

Knotted 5–6 mm cotton cords or 15–20 mm grosgrain ribbons work well up to roughly 2.5–3.0 kg when anchored through a reinforced turnover. For heavier multi-bottle sets, metal eyelets prevent the cord knot from pulling through the punched hole, while glued-in ribbon tabs eliminate visible knots on the inside wall. imageAlt: Custom die-cut EVA foam insert inside a rigid presentation box
title: Foam Inserts for Packaging: EVA vs. EPE vs. PU Comparison
seoTitle: Foam Inserts for Packaging: EVA vs EPE vs PU | MTT
summary: Compare EVA, EPE, and PU foam inserts for custom rigid boxes: density, die-cut edge precision, surface scuffing, cost, and when to choose paperboard instead.
intro: Choose EVA foam (38–45 kg/m³) when you need crisp die-cut edges, velvet flocking, and firm retention for luxury glass bottles or instruments. Choose EPE (expanded polyethylene) when cost and shock absorption in shipping cartons matter more than visual presentation, and reserve soft open-cell PU foam for lightweight items that need gentle compression. Always test filled glass containers in the exact foam cavity to check label scuffing and finger-notch removal.
faq: What density of EVA foam is standard for luxury rigid boxes?

Most cosmetics, fragrance, and electronics presentation boxes use 38–45 kg/m³ closed-cell EVA foam. Lower densities feel spongy and tear around thin bridges, while 60 kg/m³+ feels overly stiff for finger-pull removal.
Can EVA foam inserts be velvet flocked?

Yes. A thin rayon or nylon flock sheet can be laminated onto the top surface of EVA before die-cutting, or the entire molded cavity can be flocked. Note that die-cut vertical walls still show the base EVA colour unless CNC-routed or flocked post-cut.
cta: Send your product CAD or photos, filled weight, target box style, quantity per design, and destination to compare EVA, EPE, and paperboard insert options. Minimum 1,000 pieces per design and US$2,000 product value per order, excluding freight, samples, and other fees.
sections: EVA vs. EPE vs. PU: how they behave in production

EVA (Ethylene-Vinyl Acetate) is a closed-cell cross-linked foam with a smooth, fine-cell surface. It holds tight ±0.5 mm die-cut tolerances, supports velvet flocking or paper lamination on top, and resists crumbling. It is the most expensive of the three but standard for custom EVA foam insert rigid boxes.

EPE (Expanded Polyethylene) has a visible bead-like cell structure and lower unit cost. It absorbs repeated transit impacts well in outer corrugated cartons, though its rougher cut edge looks utilitarian inside a retail gift box. PU (Polyurethane) is an open-cell sponge foam that compresses easily around irregular shapes, but yellows under UV light and offers less lateral support for heavy glass.
Design rules for cavity bridges and finger notches

Leave at least 8–10 mm of foam wall between adjacent bottle cavities and 10–12 mm between any cavity and the outer rigid box wall; thinner bridges tear during die-cutting or bottle insertion. Add opposing semi-circular finger notches (14–18 mm wide) on heavy or snug-fitting items so customers can lift the product without prying at the label.
When to switch from foam to paperboard or molded pulp

If your target market enforces strict plastic-reduction rules or EU PPWR recyclability targets, a multi-layered 350 gsm SBS paperboard cradle or wet-pressed molded pulp tray can replace EVA while keeping mono-material paper recycling. Compare both paths in our EVA vs. paperboard inserts guide.

title: Emboss vs. Deboss on Rigid Boxes: Tooling, Paper Weight & Limits
seoTitle: Emboss vs Deboss on Rigid Boxes: Tooling & Paper | MTT
summary: Understand emboss vs. deboss on rigid boxes and folding cartons: brass vs. magnesium dies, paper weight limits, and why debossing is preferred on greyboard.
intro: On paper-wrapped rigid boxes, blind debossing (recessing the logo) is far more common than embossing (raising it) because rigid greyboard cannot be stamped cleanly from the back once laminated. To emboss a rigid box lid, the 120–157 gsm wrapping paper must be stamped flat before wrapping—requiring careful registration and risking crush during box assembly. Folding cartons (300–400 gsm) can be embossed or debossed in-line with brass or magnesium dies.
faq: Why is debossing easier than embossing on a rigid gift box?

Debossing presses a heated or unheated male die directly into the finished wrapped lid or flat wrap, creating a crisp shadow recess. Embossing requires a matched male-and-female die set on flat sheets before wrapping, and the raised paper dome can flatten under box-making rollers.
What minimum line weight works for blind debossing?

Keep positive lines at least 0.35–0.5 mm wide and avoid ultra-fine serif text under 8 pt. Coated art papers with matte lamination hold sharp edges, while long-fiber cotton or specialty papers give a softer, deeper impression.
cta: Share your vector logo artwork, preferred box structure, wrapping paper choice, quantity per design, and destination for a tooling and finishing check. Minimum 1,000 pieces per design and US$2,000 product value per order, excluding freight, samples, and other fees.
sections: Pre-wrap stamping vs. post-wrap debossing

When wrapping a 1,200 gsm greyboard lid, the wrap sheet passes through glue rollers and corner-turning brushes. Any raised embossed area on that thin 157 gsm wrap can get partially crushed or misaligned against the lid center. By contrast, blind debossing or blind deboss on specialty paper can be stamped cleanly with a single brass die, delivering consistent depth without registration drift.
Brass dies vs. magnesium dies

Magnesium (or zinc) dies cost less upfront and work well for short runs or simple flat debosses. CNC-engraved brass dies cost more but last through 50,000+ impressions, hold sharper 45-degree bevels, and are mandatory for multi-level sculpted embossing or combined foil-and-emboss (registering hot foil and raised relief in one pass).
Preventing paper cracking and laminate lift

Deep embossing on 350 gsm folding cartons can crack coated surfaces if the die edges are too sharp or the paper grain runs perpendicular to the longest stroke. Softening the die shoulder slightly and using a tougher 157 gsm wrap or long-fiber dyed paper prevents white stress lines around the logo.

imageAlt: Packaging dieline layout showing cut, crease, bleed, and foil layers
title: Dieline Artwork Setup: Bleed, Crease & Glue-Flap Rules
seoTitle: Dieline Artwork Setup: Bleed, Crease & Glue Flaps | MTT
summary: Prepare production-ready dielines for folding cartons and rigid boxes: 3 mm bleed, spot-colour technical layers, glue-flap knockouts, and wrap turn-ins.
intro: A production-ready packaging dieline separates structural cut and crease lines from printed artwork on locked, non-printing spot-colour layers. Extend all background colours and images at least 3 mm past the outer cut line (bleed), keep critical text 3–4 mm inside fold lines (safety margin), and leave glue flaps free of ink and lamination so hot-melt or cold-PVA adhesives bond reliably.
faq: How much bleed does a packaging dieline need?

Use a minimum of 3 mm (0.125 in) bleed past all outer die-cut edges for folding cartons, and 15–18 mm wrap turn-in allowance on rigid box wrapping sheets so the paper folds cleanly over the greyboard edge.
Why must glue flaps be kept free of ink and lamination?
Standard aqueous varnish, UV coating, and BOPP lamination block carton glue from penetrating the paperboard fibers, causing side seams or bottom flaps to pop open in transit.
cta: Send your product dimensions and target box style to receive a custom dieline template, or share your existing AI/PDF artwork for a preflight check. Minimum 1,000 pieces per design and US$2,000 product value per order, excluding freight, samples, and other fees.
sections: Separate structural layers from print layers

Always build your Adobe Illustrator or PDF file with distinct, clearly named layers: Dieline_Cut (solid line, spot colour), Dieline_Crease (dashed line, spot colour), Foil_Stamp or Spot_UV (100% K or dedicated spot swatch set to overprint), and Artwork. Never flatten the dieline into the CMYK image layer, or the cut lines will print on the press sheet.
Folding carton glue-flap and safety-margin rules

On tuck-end folding cartons, knock out all ink, varnish, and film lamination on the side glue flap, leaving a 1.5–2 mm ink-free buffer inside the crease so adhesive wets raw board fibers. Keep barcodes, ingredient panels, and logos at least 3 mm away from crease lines to prevent distortion when the board folds. For rigid box wraps, allow 15–18 mm turn-in margin around the greyboard flat. Review our artwork preflight checklist before sending files.

imageAlt: Corrugated fiberboard mailer and shipping carton flute profile comparison
title: Corrugated Fiberboard Guide: Flute Profiles, ECT & Mailer Fit
seoTitle: Corrugated Fiberboard: Flute Profiles & ECT Guide | MTT
summary: Select the right corrugated fiberboard for e-commerce mailers and master cartons: compare E, B, C, and BC double-wall flutes alongside ECT edge-crush ratings.
intro: Select corrugated fiberboard by matching flute thickness and Edge Crush Test (ECT) rating to your shipping method. Use E-flute (approx. 1.5–1.8 mm) for printed retail mailers needing crisp graphics, B-flute (approx. 2.5–3.0 mm) for heavier subscription boxes, and C-flute (approx. 3.5–4.0 mm) or BC double-wall (approx. 6.0–7.0 mm) for export master cartons stacked on pallets.
faq: What is the difference between 32 ECT and 44 ECT corrugated board?

32 ECT (Edge Crush Test) is standard for single-wall parcel mailers carrying up to roughly 15–20 kg depending on box size, while 44 ECT uses heavier linerboard and medium to resist higher stacking loads in warehouse pallets.
Which flute is best for custom printed e-commerce mailer boxes?

E-flute (1.5–1.8 mm) is the standard choice for custom printed roll-end tuck-front mailers because its tight flute pitch gives a smoother surface for litho-lamination or direct flexo printing without heavy washboarding.

sections: Compare E, B, C, and BC double-wall flutes

Flute size controls both wall thickness and crush resistance. E-flute (1.5–1.8 mm) folds cleanly for compact corrugated mailer boxes and litho-laminated retail cartons. B-flute (2.5–3.0 mm) adds puncture resistance for heavier glass or metal kits. C-flute (3.5–4.0 mm) and BC double-wall (6.0–7.0 mm) are built for export master cartons that must survive container humidity and multi-tier pallet stacking.
ECT vs. Mullen burst strength

Modern export packaging typically specifies ECT (Edge Crush Test, e.g., 32 ECT or 44 ECT) because it measures top-to-bottom stacking strength directly. Mullen burst testing (e.g., 200# test) measures puncture resistance against sharp impacts inside parcel sorters. For heavy glass fragrance or skincare shipments, pair a 32–44 ECT outer carton with internal foam inserts or corrugated dividers.
Account for board thickness in internal vs. external dimensions

A 3 mm B-flute wall adds 6 mm across length and width—and up to 12 mm on double-tuck side walls. Always specify whether your dimensions are internal (ID) or external (OD) when requesting a dieline, and verify outer carton fit using our internal vs. external box measurement guide.
